extracted.intended_audience: general readers interested in physical health and animal husbandry; parents, school-teachers, horse owners, grooms, and stable managers
extracted.subtask_description: Practical and physiological guidance for caring for horses' feet and for shoeing (and related stable/work practices) so as to preserve health, prevent injury, and prolong useful life. Also includes related general advice on human diet/physical education reflected earlier in the same page.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principal meal timing
rubrics_metrics.description: But that principal meal should be the last.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The main/ principal meal ought to be the evening meal so the stomach has time to digest before the next replenishment; allow several hours (e.g., meal at half-past four or five, conclude before six, then hours for digestion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Digest thoroughly before replenishing
rubrics_metrics.description: It is an important rule that we should digest our food thoroughly before we replenish the stomach.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To counteract overeating prefer lengthening interval between meals rather than emetics, stimulants, or other artificial aids; wait until appetite returns rather than forcing food or using harsh drugs or alcohol to stimulate digestion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lengthen interval between meals / limited number of meals
rubrics_metrics.description: Lengthen the interval between meals. Two meals a day are enough, perhaps more than enough...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Human system is highly plastic to habit — training can reduce number of meals comfortably; many historical/ethnic patterns range from one to five meals, but two (or one and two halves) is advocated as sufficient for most people.

rubrics_metrics.name: Light, simple breakfast
rubrics_metrics.description: The lightest breakfast is the best — buckwheat-cakes with a little honey or apple-butter, and a glass of milk, or a cup of chocolate, if you must take 'something warm.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer minimal, nutritive breakfasts; chocolate has nutritive properties (unlike tea/coffee per se), but overall keep breakfast light to avoid midday somnolence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid stimulants, pocket-flasks, and heavy mid-day drinking
rubrics_metrics.description: Never keep a pocket-flask. Don't stay with flagons; better comfort with apples, if you can not wait till five.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid carrying alcohol for interim relief; prefer fruit (apples, biscuits) to flagons or cocktails between meals; for children, a biscuit and apples at recess suffice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Schoolchildren recess and midday food management
rubrics_metrics.description: School-children should pass their recess on the playground. A biscuit and a pocketful of apples will satisfy the temporary demands of the stomach... they will find it far easier to forego their noonday lunch altogether than to resist the insidious somnolence which would dull their wits after a regular dinner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage physical activity during recess and small, light snacks rather than a full mid-day meal to avoid postprandial sleepiness that impairs afternoon lessons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not force children to eat; let children eat their fill at principal meal
rubrics_metrics.description: But at the principal meal they should eat their fill. ... I repeat, never press them to eat — for principle's sake — not even your young visitors; they are not likely to go to bed hungry if your menu comprises such items as baked apples or bread-pudding and sweet milk.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow natural appetite to guide intake; if a child dawdles with food when full, divert them to activity rather than coercion; provide light desserts so guests won't go hungry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer natural dietary instincts to complex medical precepts
rubrics_metrics.description: Nature's health laws are simple. The road to health and happiness is not the labyrinthine maze described by our medical mystagogues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow innate dietetic instincts and simple, ascertainable causes/effects rather than complicated, arbitrary, or anti-natural restrictions and remedies. Remedial instincts and self-regulation will often guide correct choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use fruit and simple foods in hot/sickly seasons
rubrics_metrics.description: In the sultry dog-days your system craves a surcease of greasy ragouts and yearns for something refreshing — sherbet or cool fruit. ... Fruit is a better antiseptic than fusel poison and wormwood.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In hot weather or after salt-heavy diets, prefer fruit and cool refreshments (watermelon, lemon-juice, fresh fruit) over heavy/meat-based or alcoholic remedies; avoid unnecessary antiseptic regimens like quinine unless indicated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim for long useful life of horses
rubrics_metrics.description: A horse should live from thirty-five to forty years, and live actively and usefully during three fourths of this period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Current practice (many horses destroyed under twelve years) is wasteful; caregivers/owners should aim by improved management to approach natural longevity and long active use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blame neglect and ignorance rather than horses' nature
rubrics_metrics.description: The blame must be apportioned to the degree of carelessness with which evils affecting either men or horses are allowed to go on unchecked... the blame is ours, and ours alone, if we fail to apply the remedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Owners and grooms must recognize that most horse suffering is human-caused and is remediable through informed practice rather than being inherent to the animal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grooms should not administer secret medicines
rubrics_metrics.description: It is a miserable fact that grooms on their own responsibility are in the habit of administering secretly to horses medicines ... arsenic, antimony, and niter seem to be the favorites.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prohibit unsupervised, ill-judged medication by stable staff; such treatments usually create worse mischief than the ailment and reflect ignorance rather than veterinary judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hoof porosity: avoid occlusive hoof-ointments
rubrics_metrics.description: In profound ignorance that the hoof is porous, they apply hoof-ointments, which answer to cement plastered on a wall. If these were in constant use... not a morsel of sound horn would remain at the end of six months.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not smear hooves with tar, beeswax, tallow, or similar occlusive substances that prevent internal moisture from reaching the outer surface and obstruct air circulation; such treatments lead to dryness, brittleness, and horn loss.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid constant litter bedding that softens feet and causes swelling
rubrics_metrics.description: The constant use of litter makes the feet tender and causes swelled legs... legs swell and unswell by leaving litter or taking it away.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not allow horses to be bedded down on heaps of litter all day; excessive littering softens feet and promotes swelling of the legs. Stable management should ensure appropriate footing and periods of firm contact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimize iron weight and number of nails in shoeing
rubrics_metrics.description: The efforts of all have been directed toward diminishing the weight of iron, and this has led them to the conclusion that the less the natural foot is interfered with the better.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Modern shoers aim to reduce iron weight and number of nails because heavy shoes and many nails compress hoof structure, impede natural function, and cause long-term damage; favor lighter, less obtrusive shoeing when necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow natural expansion and contraction of the hoof in shoe design
rubrics_metrics.description: The unshod foot... had expanded one eighth part of an inch at the heel and quarters... the expansion was only lateral. It would follow that a shoe intended to give full play to this process must be confined to the part where no expansion takes place.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shoes should be designed/placed so as not to inhibit the lateral expansion/contraction of the hoof on weight-bearing; confine rigid elements to non-expanding regions to preserve natural holding and withdrawal functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid paring heels and inserting excessive wedges/nails
rubrics_metrics.description: M. la Fosse... directed that the heel should be pared, thus making it weaker... fastening on his tip... with eight nails... inserting wedges... and killing it from the clinches downward and outward.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not pare heels to weaken structure or overuse nails/wedges that compress horn-tubes; such practices close pores, reduce circulation, and create brittleness and structural failure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize shoes cannot fully substitute for appropriate road/pavement design
rubrics_metrics.description: If any one method be likely to supersede the rest, the victory will probably be for the asphalt; but horses are found to slip seriously upon it... On the one hand it is urged that there should be a uniform system of paving... on the other the contention is that the true remedy lies... in the discovery of a shoe which shall effectually prevent the horse from slipping anywhere. The former alternative is visionary...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While ideal pavement uniformity is impractical, shoeing should strive to accommodate varied surfaces; however, owners and city planners should be aware that pavement choice and vehicle braking design (e.g., breaks on wagons) also materially affect horse safety and wear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prevent unnecessary strain from vehicle design and work practices
rubrics_metrics.description: A horse should not be obliged to work in going down a hill... they are subject to the severest strain just when they ought to have none, if they are harnessed to springless carts or wagons without brakes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design and use vehicles (brakes, springs) and assign work practices so horses aren't forced into excessive strain (e.g., downhill braking by the animal). Reducing mechanical causes of slipping and shaking will reduce foot and musculoskeletal disease.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be cautious and gradual in adopting changes to shoeing
rubrics_metrics.description: They will not be told that unless they abandon the system of shoeing altogether they can effect no improvement... On the contrary, they will find... warned against imprudent haste, and are told that a vast amount of good may be achieved even if they never venture on leaving of their horses' feet in a state of nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt improvements in shoeing cautiously; substantial benefits can be realized by incremental reductions in iron and nailing even without abandoning shoeing altogether. Consider evidence and avoid rash wholesale abandonment without practical trials.
